title: If finding backtested strategies is so easy…
author: vesomortex
selftext:
Why do you think so few are actually using the same ones as trading algorithms? 

Food for thought.

It’s very easy to find a backtested strategy that works, and yet we aren’t all billionaires and most of the people trying to make money are the ones selling shovels. 

Maybe it’s a hell of a lot harder than you could possibly think to get a strategy that actually works in the real world.

comments.author: Party_Musician_9914
comments.body:
I agree with the central point: finding an attractive historical equity curve is much easier than proving a durable, executable edge.

But I don’t think “why isn’t everyone using the same algorithm?” is the right test. Markets don’t have one universally correct strategy. Traders have different capital, costs, execution, holding periods, drawdown limits and access to data. Some edges also have limited capacity or weaken once widely exploited.

A backtest should be treated as the beginning of an investigation—not the finished product. The difficult work is controlling overfitting, testing genuinely unseen regimes, stressing costs and execution, using realistic sizing and then surviving a meaningful forward test.

That doesn’t mean working algorithms don’t exist. It means the valuable part isn’t finding a strategy that performed historically; it’s demonstrating that the underlying edge is robust enough to survive contact with reality.

replies.author: vesomortex
replies.body: No my point is why isn’t everyone using -an- algorithm or AI? Not the same one. Because it isn’t that easy

replies.author: Party_Musician_9914
replies.body: Fair point—it definitely isn’t easy. That’s actually why I spent roughly four years developing my own rather than expecting an off-the-shelf AI to trade profitably for me. It doesn’t remove uncertainty, but it gives me consistent execution, removes much of the emotion and saves me from living in front of charts. AI is a development tool; it isn’t the edge by itself.

replies.author: Working_Pollution_71
replies.body: I think its easy made 150$ in 2 days and broke schwab api limits lol

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
Two different things get called "a backtest that works". One is a curve that looks good after you tried fifty variants, which is mostly selection. The other is a rule that still behaves the same on data it never saw, and those are rare.

Even the rare ones then meet the boring layer: a feed that gaps, a ticker that halts, a bot that quietly stops placing orders and looks healthy on every dashboard. None of that shows up in a backtest, and in my experience it is where most of the live gap comes from.

So I'd agree, and add that the hard part is less the math than keeping the thing honest for months.

comments.author: NefariousnessOpening
comments.body: Back testing can work or it can degrade the system. It seems like a common misconception that back testing can be applied to any strategy development process. Knowing when to use it and more importantly the precise data engineering methodology is necessary to ensure the desired outcome is even possible

comments.author: AdBitter6080
comments.body: The hard part isn't finding a backtest that works; it's keeping it honest for months. A 'backtest that works' is often just a curve-fitted result to historical noise. The real edge is rarely in the rule itself, but in the data engineering and execution infrastructure—handling gaps, halts, and engine failures—that most backtests conveniently ignore. Practical takeaway: Focus more on execution robustness than on tightening entry criteria.

comments.author: Interesting-Bet-769
comments.body: It’s not just finding it, it has to out perform buy & hold of SPY live or you don’t have an edge.

comments.author: bufflo8
comments.body:
Exactly—the hard part isn’t finding a profitable backtest; it’s proving the edge survives out-of-sample data, fees, slippage and changing market conditions without overfitting. If everyone uses it, the edge can also disappear.

That’s partly why I’m building [bufflo.io](https://bufflo.io/?utm_source=reddit). Its AI agent can build indicators, screeners and alerts, analyse tickers, customise workspaces and backtest ideas, with trading on the same platform. I’d appreciate your feedback on which real-world validation tools matter most.

comments.author: Less-Bad-9124
comments.body: I think the gap is between finding a pattern in historical data and proving that the pattern represents something durable enough to survive live execution. Once you add spreads, slippage, latency, changing regimes and the fact that other participants adapt, a lot of beautiful backtests get ordinary very quickly. It’s something I keep in mind when testing ideas around Moon too and the backtest is evidence worth investigating, not proof that you’ve found an edge.

comments.author: Think-Bench6691
comments.body:
In my experience it's very easy to find something that works. But it's nearly impossible to consistently predict if/when it stops working.

The only consistent way to know something stopped working is by losing a lot of money.
